report.releaseDate: 3 Nov 2026 (NGB National Gambling Statistics FY2025/26, period 1 Apr 2025–31 Mar 2026; NGB Annual Report 2025/26 published Oct 2026)
report.currency: ZAR (R) — tables in R bn unless stated; ~USD alongside at USD/ZAR 16.5 (ESTIMATE — see confidence note)
report.verdict: South Africa's regulated gambling market set a record R84.46bn (~$5.12bn) GGR in FY2025/26 (+13.4%), but the growth is a single engine — online sports betting (R55.77bn, +25%) licensed province-by-province and taxed at ~6.5% of GGR plus VAT. The rules are now moving against the grain of that growth: the SCA has shut the bookmaker 'casino-game' loophole, Treasury wants a 20% national online GGR tax with the design due in the Feb-2027 Budget, advertising norms are drafted, and a site-blocking tender is live — while online casino stays illegal and an estimated majority of online play sits offshore. Attractive scale, deteriorating rule-set.
summary: **Record year, decelerating.** The NGB's audited FY2025/26 statistics (1 Apr 2025–31 Mar 2026) put gross gambling revenue (GGR = stakes less winnings, before tax) at R84.46bn (~$5.12bn), +13.4% on R74.50bn (~$4.52bn). Growth has slowed from +25.7% (FY23/24) and +25.6% (FY24/25). The headline is corroborated by Gaming Intelligence, The Citizen, News24/GroundUp and Daily Maverick (all R84.46–84.5bn).

**One engine: betting delivered more than 100% of growth.** Betting GGR rose R10.18bn (~$617m) to R62.16bn (~$3.77bn, +19.6%) while casinos (-R142m), bingo (-R186m) and LPMs (+R110m) netted to a decline. Betting is 73.6% of GGR (50% three years ago; 12% in FY11/12); casinos 19.5%, LPMs 5.0%, bingo 1.8%.

**Online penetration is at least 66% of the whole market.** In the six provinces that disaggregate it (WC, MP, LP, NW, EC, NC) online betting GGR was R55.77bn (~$3.38bn), +25.4%, equal to 66.0% of total GGR and 89.7% of betting GGR; retail betting fell 15.0% to R6.39bn (~$387m). Gauteng, KZN and Free State are not split, so true online share is higher. Daily Maverick reports mobile at 91% of digital wagering.

**Stakes of R1.76tn (~$106.9bn), +17.5%.** Betting turnover was R1.40tn (~$84.9bn, +24.5%), 79.5% of all money wagered and ~57x the R24.5bn of FY2013/14 (News24). Market hold on betting is 4.4% (RTP 95.6%); sports bookmaking hold 4.1%; casino hold 5.9% on R280.5bn (~$17.0bn) of turnover (-4.2%).

**Tax take R6.45bn (~$391m), +10.9% — growth is in the lowest-taxed mode.** Provincial taxes/levies on GGR: betting R4.11bn (~$249m, 6.6% effective), casinos R1.66bn (~$100m, 10.0%), LPMs R543m (~$33m, 12.7%), bingo R132m (~$8m, 8.5%). Betting generates 74% of GGR but 64% of tax. These figures exclude VAT (15% applies to betting), corporate tax and the National Lottery.

**Tax regime is provincial and GGR-based, with VAT on top.** Nine Provincial Licensing Authorities (PLAs) levy tax under provincial Acts: Gauteng bookmakers 6.5% of gross betting revenue + 1% Sports Development Fund levy; casinos 9% (Gauteng) or 8–19% progressive (Western Cape); LPM route operators 15% (Gauteng) / 10–20% (WC); bingo 12% / 10–15%. Treasury characterises bookmaker taxation as 6–7% (elsewhere 6–9%) of GGR; player winnings are untaxed unless habitual income.

**The 20% national online gambling tax is the dominant swing factor.** Treasury's Nov-2025 discussion paper proposes a separate national 20% tax on online betting and interactive GGR, in addition to provincial taxes (combined 26–29% before VAT), SARS-administered, worth '>R10bn' (~$606m) at current GGR and framed as a 'sin tax'. The Finance Minister's MTBPS (21 Oct 2026) deferred final design to the Feb-2027 Budget; industry models an all-in burden approaching 40% of GGR including VAT; passage requires a money bill through both houses and the DA (a GNU partner) has opposed it.

**Legal framework: a 2004 statute, concurrent competence, no online casino.** Gambling is a concurrent national/provincial competence (Constitution Sched. 4). National Gambling Act 7 of 2004 s11 prohibits interactive gambling; the 2008 Amendment Act that would have created national online licences was never proclaimed; the National Gambling Amendment Bill is stalled (NGB AR cites 'delayed enactment'); the Remote Gambling Bill (B11-2024, DA private member's bill) is not expected before 2027. Only fixed-odds betting on sport, horse racing and 'other contingencies' via a provincial bookmaker licence is lawful online.

**The SCA closed the 'casino games as fixed-odds bets' loophole.** Portapa (Pty) Ltd t/a Supabets v Casino Association of SA [2025] ZASCA 158 (21 Oct 2025) held that under the Gauteng Gambling Act bookmakers may not offer fixed-odds bets on casino games including roulette. NGB then advised dtic/NRCS that Remote Gaming Servers are unlawful under s11; NRCS stopped issuing or renewing Letters of Certification for RGS products under SANS 1718. The data shows the hit: Gauteng betting GGR -19.2% to R3.77bn (~$228m), quarterly betting turnover collapsed from R8.46bn (Q1) to R2.34bn (Q3), and Gauteng betting RTP fell from 88% to 61–73% in H2 as high-RTP casino-style content was withdrawn.

**Licensing geography drives the numbers.** Mpumalanga (GGR R29.23bn, ~$1.77bn, 34.6% share, +31.4%) and Western Cape (R24.66bn, ~$1.49bn, 29.2%) host the major online bookmakers' primary licences and collect 59% of all gambling tax (R1.94bn and R1.86bn). Eastern Cape (betting GGR +676% to R1.46bn) and North West (+205% to R1.29bn) show new licensees locating there. Gauteng's share of GGR fell to 14.6% (-8.4%). Effective betting tax: WC 6.4%, MP 6.6%, GP 7.0%, KZN 10.5%.

**Operator landscape: an online duopoly, a land-based oligopoly.** 315 operational bookmakers (539 outlets), 340 tote outlets, 36 casinos, 2,594 LPM site operators, 62 bingo halls. Blask demand data had Betway and Hollywoodbets at >75% of online demand (Mar-2025), with Hollywoodbets ~27% by Feb-2026 and Betway gaining 4.8pp; Q1-2026 traffic data puts Betway, YesPlay and Hollywoodbets at ~50% of 380m visits. Sun International's SunBet grew income 35.5% to R1.18bn (~$72m) in H1-2026 'ahead of market growth of ~19%'. Tsogo Sun (15), Sun International (11) and Peermont (8) own 34 of 36 casinos; Sun holds 49.0% land-based casino share.

**Land-based is ex-growth but stabilising.** Casino GGR R16.50bn (~$1.00bn), -0.9%, but Q3 +0.8% and Q4 +6.7% YoY; gambling positions fell to 24,246 (from 28,362), slots 20,981, tables 865. LPMs are the resilient land-based product: 15,988 machines (+1.6%), GGR R4.26bn (~$258m, +2.6%). Bingo is in structural decline: GGR -10.7%, outlets 73→62, EBTs 8,868→8,413.

**Lottery sits outside the NGB numbers and is in legal limbo.** Sizekhaya Holdings took over the National Lottery and sports pools on 1 Jun 2026 under the fourth licence (Ithuba had operated since 2015 plus a 12-month temporary term); on 3 Nov 2026 the Pretoria High Court set aside the licence award and declared the licence agreement invalid — operator continuity is now uncertain.

**Payments are bank-rail, not mobile-money.** Licensed operators run on cards, instant EFT and retail vouchers; offshore sites also accept rands, local cards and digital vouchers (Daily Maverick). Exchange-control rules require Authorised Dealers to refuse FX for offshore gambling and residents may not use cards for it; s16 NGA lets banks withhold illegal winnings for the NGB (R775k ~$47k forfeited in FY25/26; ~R3m ~$182k cumulative). The FIC has been AML/CFT supervisor of gambling since Dec-2022 and has now signed MOUs with the NGB and all PLAs.

**The illegal online market is large and currently unblockable.** Yield Sec estimates ~62% of online activity on unlicensed sites, >R50bn (~$3.0bn) GGR offshore and ~16m users; CGCSA puts tax leakage at ~R7.7bn (~$467m)/yr. The NGB restricted 27 illegal sites, ran 35 enforcement interventions, and issued an EOI (30 Jun 2026; closed 4 Sep 2026) for a national monitoring/tracking/blocking solution; the Communications Minister is exploring Icasa network-level powers, which gaming lawyers argue are ultra vires.

**Advertising and RG are tightening, slowly.** s15 NGA and reg. 3 bar ads aimed at minors and require RG messaging; the NGB has issued directives to PLAs and is drafting national advertising norms and standards; dtic promised norms and regulations 'before July 2026' but none had been gazetted by mid-Aug 2026. Civil-society petitions seek a tobacco-style ban on ads and sponsorships. The National Self-Exclusion Register remains inoperative 22 years after the Act; the NRGP helpline logged 1.26m calls and the NRGF treated 3,541 people in FY25/26. NGB flags escalation among NSFAS students and SASSA grant recipients; StatsSA puts gambling at 54.5% of household recreation/culture spend.

**Regulatory fragmentation is itself a risk.** The NGB reports an open dispute with certain PLAs over s11 (licensed operators 'engaging in prohibited gambling activities'), escalated to the National Gambling Policy Council under ss62–63; it issued only 9 of 45 planned PLA compliance evaluations (20%). Gauteng data in the stats is provisional/unaudited.

**Read-through for B2Tech.** This is Africa's largest regulated market (~$5.1bn GGR; >$3.4bn disclosed online) with a low headline tax, deep card/EFT/voucher rails and lawful online sports betting — but it is a sports-only licence, the casino upsell is judicially closed, the fiscal burden could roughly double from April 2027, and advertising/sponsorship rules are tightening. The practical route is a Western Cape or Mpumalanga bookmaker licence (modest fees; B-BBEE, probity and SANS 1718 testing; 3–12 month timelines), a mobile-first sports book with 'other contingencies' products that survive s11 scrutiny, and an entry case stress-tested at 26–40% all-in tax against an entrenched Betway/Hollywoodbets duopoly.

segments.name: Sports betting & horse racing (online + retail bookmakers, totalisators)
segments.headline: R62.16bn (~$3.77bn) GGR, +19.6%; online R55.77bn (+25.4%) is ~90% of betting; growth decelerating, Gauteng shrinking post-SCA, Mpumalanga/WC licence hubs now 80% of betting GGR.
narrative: Betting GGR reached R62.16bn (~$3.77bn) in FY2025/26, +19.6%, against +44.7% and +51.2% in the two prior years — still the fastest-growing mode but on a visibly flattening curve. Fixed-odds bookmaking on sport and 'other contingencies' is the business: R56.78bn (~$3.44bn), +18.6%, or 91% of betting GGR. The surprise is bookmaker horse-racing GGR at R4.81bn (~$292m), +36.9% on turnover of R13.5bn (~$821m) — almost all of it booked in the Western Cape (R4.49bn), where Q3/Q4 horse-racing GGR jumped to R1.34–1.37bn per quarter from ~R0.9bn; the totalisator (4Racing in WC, Gold Circle in KZN) is marginal at R0.56bn (~$34m), -0.7%, with the NGB flagging tote B-BBEE non-compliance (average level 6.4). Betting taxes rose 20.2% to R4.11bn (~$249m), an effective 6.6% of GGR nationally (sports bookmaking 6.4%, horse racing 9.2%).

The channel shift is nearly complete. Online betting GGR in the six provinces that disclose it was R55.77bn (~$3.38bn), +25.4%, while retail betting fell 15.0% to R6.39bn (~$387m); bookmaker shopfronts fell from 553 to 539 even as tote outlets rose to 340. Because Gauteng, KZN and Free State do not split online from retail, the 66.0% online share of total GGR is a floor, and the Daily Maverick's 91% mobile share of digital wagering is consistent with a market where the smartphone, not the shop or the casino floor, is the point of sale. Hold is thin and falling: betting RTP rose to 95.6% (92.0% in FY24/25), giving a market hold of 4.4% on R1.40tn (~$84.9bn) of stakes, and 4.1% on the R1.386tn sports book — stakes grew 24.5% but GGR only 19.6%.

The quarterly profile shows the regulatory shock. Betting GGR growth was +23.3% (Q1), +23.0% (Q2), +13.8% (Q3, Oct–Dec 2025) and +19.7% (Q4). Q3 is the quarter the SCA handed down Portapa t/a Supabets v Casino Association of SA (21 Oct 2025), outlawing fixed-odds bets on roulette and other casino games under the Gauteng Gambling Act, followed by the NRCS halting certification of Remote Gaming Servers. Gauteng betting turnover collapsed from R8.46bn in Q1 to R2.34bn in Q3 (-72%), Gauteng betting GGR slid from R1.01bn to R0.84bn by Q4 (full year R3.77bn, -19.2%), and Gauteng betting RTP fell from 88% to 61% (Q3) and 73% (Q4) — exactly what one expects when high-RTP casino-style content is pulled from a bookmaker product set. Elsewhere, growth continued: Mpumalanga betting GGR hit R7.65bn in Q3 and the Western Cape R5.83bn in Q4. The judgment is formally confined to Gauteng's Act, but the NGB has adopted its logic nationally and is in a formal s11 dispute with 'certain PLAs' now before the National Gambling Policy Council — the regulatory status of lucky-numbers, virtuals and 'betgames'-type products outside Gauteng is the live question for any entrant.

Provincial numbers reveal where licences, not punters, live. Mpumalanga booked R28.35bn (~$1.72bn) of betting GGR (45.6% of the national total, +33.0%) and the Western Cape R21.18bn (~$1.28bn, 34.1%, +8.5%); Limpopo R4.16bn (+5.1%); Gauteng R3.77bn (-19.2%); KZN R1.40bn (-8.1%); Eastern Cape R1.46bn (+676%) and North West R1.29bn (+205%) from negligible bases, and Northern Cape R0.48bn (+66%). This is licence migration: a bookmaker licensed in any province may take bets from residents nationwide, so operators domicile where processing, rates and supervision suit them. Effective betting tax rates by province were WC 6.4%, MP 6.6%, Gauteng 7.0%, Limpopo 6.5%, EC 6.6%, NW 5.0% and KZN 10.5% — the spread explains why KZN, home of Hollywoodbets' retail roots, has only 2.3% of betting GGR.

Competitively the online book is a duopoly with a long tail. Blask demand data had Betway and Hollywoodbets at more than three-quarters of online demand in March 2025, with Hollywoodbets around 27% by February 2026 and Betway up 4.8pp; Q1-2026 traffic analytics put Betway, YesPlay and Hollywoodbets at about half of 380m site visits, with LottoStar, World Sports Betting, Supabets and JackpotCity mid-tier. The casino groups' digital arms are the growth challengers: SunBet (Sun International) lifted income 35.5% to R1.18bn (~$72m) in the six months to June 2026, 'ahead of market growth of approximately 19%', with its online-gaming GGR +43.2% versus sports betting +10.9% — a mix that itself shows how much bookmaker growth has come from non-sport 'gaming' products now under s11 scrutiny. For a new entrant the economics are a ~4% hold sports book, 6.5% provincial tax + 1% levy + 15% VAT (~18–20% of GGR all-in today), high marketing intensity against two brands with league title sponsorships, and a product perimeter that is narrowing rather than widening.

Demand is seasonal around European football — a mid-year trough and a November–December peak on EPL/UCL fixture density plus year-end spending — with Friday-evening and Saturday peaks (Blask). Horse racing is a Western Cape and Gauteng phenomenon. The NGB notes gambling 'as a substitute for income' among NSFAS student-allowance and SASSA grant recipients, which is where the advertising and affordability debate will bite first; an operator's RG design will need to anticipate payday-cycle controls and marketing limits before they are legislated.

segments.name: Land-based: casinos, LPMs & bingo
segments.headline: Casino GGR R16.50bn (~$1.00bn), -0.9% but back to growth in H2; three groups own 34 of 36 casinos; LPMs the only land-based product growing (+2.6%); bingo in structural decline (-10.7%).
narrative: Casinos generated R16.50bn (~$1.00bn) of GGR on R280.5bn (~$17.0bn) of turnover (hold 5.9%, RTP 94.1%), down 0.9% for the year but with the trend turning: quarterly GGR was -3.6% and -6.8% YoY in Q1/Q2, then +0.8% in Q3 and +6.7% in Q4 (R4.27bn). Sun International's interim to June 2026 corroborates the inflection — land-based casino income +1.5% to R3.4bn (~$206m) on 'heavy bonusing and incentive spending', with group land-based share up 2.3pp to 49.0%. Casino share of national GGR has fallen from 81% in FY2011/12 to 19.5%; the sector's statutory cap of 40 casino licences (36 operating, with Morula, Carousel, Naledi and Mayfair closed) means no capacity growth, and the floor is shrinking — operational positions fell to 24,246 from 28,362, slots to 20,981 and tables to 865. Casino taxes were R1.66bn (~$100m), -3.5%, an effective 10.0% (Gauteng 9% flat; Western Cape 8–19% progressive, KZN comparatively heavy).

Geography and ownership are concentrated. Gauteng produced R7.22bn (~$438m, 43.8%, -3.5%) — Montecasino, Gold Reef City, Silverstar and Emerald (Tsogo Sun), Time Square and Carnival City (Sun International), Emperors Palace (Peermont); KZN R3.87bn (~$235m, +9.0%, with a R1.28bn Q4 spike at Suncoast/Sibaya/Golden Horse/Black Rock/Umfolozi); Western Cape R2.56bn (~$155m, -5.0%; GrandWest, Golden Valley, Caledon, Mykonos, Garden Route); Eastern Cape R1.04bn (-5.4%). By controlling shareholder the NGB lists Tsogo Sun with 15 casinos, Sun International 11, Peermont 8, and two independents (Desert Palace, Queens). Casinos are the most transformed segment (average B-BBEE level 1.6). For a technology operator the only land-based entry points are supply/platform relationships with these groups or LPM route operation.

Limited payout machines are the resilient land-based product: 15,988 active LPMs (+1.6%) across 2,594 site operators, GGR R4.26bn (~$258m, +2.6%) at a 92.3% RTP, with Western Cape (R909m), KZN (R896m) and Gauteng (R878m) each over a fifth of the total. The NGB's National Central Electronic Monitoring System (NCEMS) captures every machine event (99.87% availability in FY25/26) and the board has streamlined Type B site applications. LPM taxes were R543m (~$33m), the highest effective rate of any mode at 12.7% (Gauteng 15%; WC 10–20%). The NGB reported it 'facilitated' R4.2bn of LPM revenue against a R2.5bn target — LPM growth is politically welcome because it is monitored, local and job-creating.

Bingo (now entirely electronic bingo terminals) is in structural decline: GGR R1.54bn (~$94m), -10.7% after -8.6% the year before; outlets fell from 73 to 62 and EBTs from 8,868 to 8,413, with play confined to Gauteng (R477m), KZN (R348m), Eastern Cape (R345m), North West, Mpumalanga and Limpopo. Taxes were R132m (~$8m), 8.5% effective. EBTs compete directly with LPMs and with mobile bookmaking for the same lower-stake customer and are losing on convenience.

The commercial implication is that land-based GGR (R22.3bn, ~$1.35bn across casino, LPM and bingo) is a mature, consolidated, capex-heavy pool with no licence headroom, whose owners are redeploying capital into digital (SunBet; Tsogo's online arm) and into bonusing to defend share. Any national online tax that exempts land-based play would widen the fiscal gap between the two channels — Treasury's paper explicitly argues casinos deserve lower rates for employment and infrastructure — and the casino lobby (Casino Association of SA was the successful litigant in the SCA case) has shown it will use the courts to defend the perimeter.

segments.name: Licensing, legal framework & tax
segments.headline: Nine provincial licensing authorities under a 2004 national Act; online casino prohibited (s11); SCA and NRCS have narrowed bookmaker product scope; Treasury's 20% national online GGR tax lands in the Feb-2027 Budget.
narrative: Gambling (casinos, racing, wagering) is a concurrent national-provincial competence under Schedule 4 of the Constitution; lotteries and sports pools are national under the Lotteries Act 1997 (National Lotteries Commission). The National Gambling Act 7 of 2004 sets national norms, creates the National Gambling Board (a dtic entity) with oversight, registers, the NCEMS, enforcement support and statistics functions, and recognises nine PLAs — Eastern Cape Gambling Board, Free State Gambling & Liquor Authority, Gauteng Gambling Board, KwaZulu-Natal Economic Regulatory Authority, Limpopo Gambling Board, Mpumalanga Economic Regulator, Northern Cape Gambling Board, North West Gambling Board and Western Cape Gambling & Racing Board — which have exclusive jurisdiction to investigate and issue provincial licences (casino, bookmaker, totalisator, route operator and LPM site, bingo, manufacturer/supplier/maintenance, key employee). Disputes between the NGB and PLAs go to the National Gambling Policy Council (ss62–63), which is where the current s11 'interactive gambling' dispute now sits. The NGB itself licenses no operators: the 2008 Amendment Act that would have given it exclusive jurisdiction over interactive licences was never proclaimed, and the later National Gambling Amendment Bill is stalled.

Online product scope is therefore defined by the bookmaker licence: fixed-odds bets on sport, horse racing and 'other contingencies', offered to residents anywhere in South Africa. Interactive casino games (RNG slots, roulette, blackjack, live dealer) are prohibited by s11 regardless of channel. The Supreme Court of Appeal in Portapa t/a Supabets v Casino Association of SA and Gauteng Gambling Board v CASA ([2025] ZASCA 158, 21 Oct 2025) held that 'sporting events' and 'contingencies' under the Gauteng Gambling Act 4 of 1995 do not include roulette, so bookmakers cannot offer fixed-odds casino games; the NGB then advised dtic and the NRCS that Remote Gaming Server architectures facilitate unlawful interactive gambling, and the NRCS directed that RGS products may no longer be submitted for SANS 1718 certification, with existing Letters of Certification lapsing on expiry. Provincial technical approval of any new product runs through accredited test labs and PLA review of three to twelve months (Daily Maverick). The DA's Remote Gambling Bill (B11-2024), which would create a national remote-gambling licence, advertising rules and player protections, was introduced in April 2024, lapsed with the sixth Parliament (one trade source) and is reported as unlikely to be enacted before 2027.

Licensing cost is not the barrier; probity, transformation and time are. Trade press cites Western Cape bookmaker fees of R15,000 (~$910) application, R3,000 (~$180) annual and R12,000 (~$730) probity/investigation, with other provinces at R10,000–20,000 application — figures we could not verify against gazetted tariffs and flag as such. There is no statutory local-ownership cap, but PLAs score applicants on the dtic B-BBEE codes (casino operators average level 1.6, LPM operators 2.4, bingo 3.1, totes 6.4), and the Mpumalanga regulator's public message to would-be entrants is 'don't come to South Africa just looking for a licence'. The practical consequence is visible in the NGB's provincial tables: Mpumalanga and the Western Cape collected R1.94bn (~$118m) and R1.86bn (~$113m) of tax (30% and 29% of the national total), while Eastern Cape, North West and Northern Cape betting GGR grew 676%, 205% and 66% as new licensees domiciled there.

Tax is levied by each province on GGR, with rates set in provincial regulations. Treasury's own table for Gauteng (GN 570 of 1997 as amended) shows bookmakers at 6.5% of gross betting revenue plus a 1% Sports Development Fund levy, horse-racing bets at 6% + 6%, totalisators 9% + 8.5%, casinos 9%, bingo 12% and route operators 15%; the Western Cape applies progressive scales — casinos 8% (<R14.2m) to 19% (>R71m), LPMs 10–20%, bingo 10–15%. Realised effective rates in FY25/26 were betting 6.6%, casinos 10.0%, LPMs 12.7%, bingo 8.5%, blended 7.6%. On top sits 15% VAT (applied to betting, which industry puts at ~12% of GGR on a VAT-inclusive basis) and 27% corporate income tax; gambling winnings are not taxed unless they constitute habitual income — the 2011 Budget's 15% withholding tax on wins above R25,000 and the 2012 Budget's 1% national levy were both abandoned. Provinces depend on national transfers for ~97% of revenue, so gambling tax is one of their few own-revenue levers — an incentive that Daily Maverick notes aligns PLAs with licensee growth.

The national online gambling tax is the reform that matters. Treasury's November 2025 discussion paper, 'The Case for a National Online Gambling Tax', proposes a separate 20% national tax on GGR from online betting including interactive gambling, additional to provincial taxes, on a uniform GGR base, administered by SARS using the returns operators already file with PLAs, and applying equally to unlicensed interactive revenue. Treasury's arithmetic: combined 26–29% of GGR, 'over R10 billion' (~$606m) of new national revenue at current GGR, with the stated objective being harm reduction rather than revenue. Written comments closed in January, extended to February 2026; the Finance Minister told Parliament in the MTBPS on 21 October 2026 that submissions 'generally recognised the need to address the growth of online gambling' and that the final design would be announced in the February 2027 Budget; Treasury then met provincial regulators and, in mid-November 2026, ~200 industry participants on a call where each had ten minutes. Industry (SA Bookmakers' Association, Whitesmans, Lurie Inc, Free Market Foundation) argues the all-in burden would approach 40% of GGR, push punters to tax-free offshore sites, erode provincial revenue and bankrupt smaller licensees; the DA has reportedly opposed it. The measure must pass as a money bill through both finance committees, the National Assembly and the NCOP, so an effective date before 1 April 2027 is implausible and slippage into FY2027/28 or dilution of the rate is realistic. Treasury's own paper concedes the Kenya precedent of operators relocating offshore when rates rose.

segments.name: Payments, responsible gambling & advertising
segments.headline: Bank-rail market (cards, instant EFT, vouchers; 91% mobile) with exchange-control and s16 forfeiture levers against offshore play; RG architecture incomplete (no self-exclusion register); advertising norms promised for July 2026 still unpublished amid ban petitions.
narrative: South Africa is not a mobile-money market in the East African sense; licensed operators fund wallets through bank cards, instant-EFT rails and retail cash vouchers, and the same rails are what offshore sites exploit — Daily Maverick notes unlicensed platforms accept rands, local cards and digital vouchers while marketing through influencers and sponsorships. The state's levers are financial rather than technical: exchange-control rules oblige Authorised Dealers to decline foreign-currency purchases for offshore gambling and bar residents from using debit or credit cards for it; under s16 of the National Gambling Act any person, including banks, who is prevented from paying unlawful winnings must remit them to the NGB in trust, with forfeiture to the State by High Court order (approximately R775,000, ~$47k, in FY25/26 and about R3m, ~$182k, cumulatively including R2.3m early in FY26/27). The NGB is pursuing MOUs with SABRIC and the SARB to attack payment flows, and the FIC — AML/CFT supervisor of gambling accountable institutions since the PLAs ceased that role in December 2022 — has now formalised information-sharing MOUs with the NGB and all nine PLAs. FICA customer due diligence (ID verification, source-of-funds on thresholds) is standard for licensed books; operators should expect bank-side transaction monitoring for gambling MCCs to tighten as the blocking programme matures.

Responsible gambling infrastructure is thinner than the market's size warrants. The industry-funded National Responsible Gambling Programme runs the 0800 006 008 helpline; the National Responsible Gambling Foundation logged 1.26m incoming calls in FY25/26, of which 5,443 were treatment-related and 3,541 people were treated — numbers that, as Daily Maverick observes, measure response capacity rather than prevalence. The NGB's own narrative is blunt: persistent unemployment and living costs have led vulnerable people to treat gambling as income substitution, with 'marked escalation' among NSFAS student-allowance and SASSA grant recipients, and StatsSA's Personal Services survey puts gambling at 54.5% of household spend on recreation, sport and culture. The National Self-Exclusion Register envisaged in the 2004 Act is still 'inoperative' (NGB AR), leaving exclusion operator-by-operator; there are no statutory deposit limits or affordability checks of the UK type. An operator building for 2027 should assume mandatory RG messaging on all marketing (already required under reg. 3), and should plan for a national exclusion feed and possibly stake/deposit controls once the Amendment Bill or advertising regulations move.

Advertising is the most politically charged file after tax. s15 NGA and regulation 3 of the National Gambling Regulations prohibit advertising directed at minors, misleading claims and ads without responsible-gambling warnings, with enforcement delegated to PLAs; the NGB recorded a 'notable increase' in gambling advertising in FY25/26, issued formal directives to PLAs to permit only compliant advertising, and is developing national advertising norms and standards. In a February 2026 parliamentary reply the dtic said it expected to publish those norms 'as well as gambling advertising regulations before July 2026'; by mid-August 2026 civil-society groups were petitioning that nothing had appeared, and the amandla.mobi campaign — which delivered a petition for a tobacco-style ban on gambling ads and sponsorships at the Betway- and Hollywoodbets-sponsored Responsible Gambling Summit in November 2025 — remains active. Communications Minister Malatsi has asked what Icasa can do under its electronic-communications mandate where networks are used to access gambling, a route gaming lawyers argue cannot create powers Parliament has not granted. The regulatory likelihood is watershed and sponsorship restrictions, bonus-advertising limits and influencer rules rather than an outright ban, but football title sponsorships — the duopoly's main brand channel — are the obvious target.

For B2Tech the payments reality is a positive (instant settlement, low fraud, card and voucher ubiquity, no telco revenue share), while the RG and advertising direction raises customer-acquisition cost and narrows channels just as a tax rise would compress contribution margin. Building the RG stack above current law — self-exclusion that interoperates with an eventual national register, affordability signals on NSFAS/SASSA pay cycles, and ad compliance reviewable by PLAs — is a licence-defensibility investment, not a cost line, given the Mpumalanga regulator's 'earn the trust' posture and the NGB's public positioning against 'gambling as a financial solution'.

segments.name: Enforcement, illegal market & political direction
segments.headline: NGB has blocked 27 sites and run 35 raids, but admits it has no blocking architecture; a monitoring/blocking tender closed 4 Sep 2026; estimates put ~62% of online activity offshore. Politics point to more tax, less advertising, and no online-casino legalisation before 2027.
narrative: The NGB's Enforcement programme completed 35 interventions in FY25/26 (raids and inspections on illegal land-based premises with SAPS arrests; 32 the prior year including 22 raids and 10 warning notices), closed targeted investigations within five days against a 25-day standard, and reports that 27 identified illegal gambling websites have been restricted for South African users through engagement with international regulators and platforms. It also concedes the limits: unlawful-winnings remittances from banks fell, there is 'no operational, state-level IP or website-blocking architecture', and effective action requires NGB–ISP–bank collaboration. On 30 June 2026 the board issued an Expression of Interest (ref. 01/2026_ED) for a monitoring, tracking, blocking and reporting solution to detect and prevent illicit online gambling, amended it on 17 July and extended the deadline to 4 September 2026 — vendor appointment and the legal basis for ISP-level blocking are the next milestones.

The scale of the illegal market is contested but large on every estimate. Yield Sec (industry-commissioned) puts roughly 62% of online gambling activity on unlicensed sites, more than R50bn (~$3.0bn) of GGR diverted offshore annually and about 16 million users; the Consumer Goods Council of SA estimates ~R7.7bn (~$467m) of direct tax loss and more than 30,000 displaced jobs. None of these is a regulator figure and we treat them as directional. The mechanics are familiar — offshore servers, Curaçao licences displayed in the footer, rand pricing, local cards and vouchers, influencer and sponsorship marketing — and the structural driver is the s11 prohibition on online casino: the only lawful supplier of RNG and live-dealer product to a South African is an unlicensed one. The SCA ruling and NRCS directive, by stripping casino-style content from licensed bookmakers, arguably increase the offshore market's relative appeal unless blocking and payment interdiction arrive quickly.

Political direction is consistent across government, if uncoordinated between its parts. Treasury wants a national 20% online GGR tax framed as a sin tax (official Christopher Axelson leads the design) and has kept it alive through the October 2026 MTBPS for the February 2027 Budget; the dtic (Minister Parks Tau) is drafting advertising norms and regulations and has not advanced legalisation of online casino; the NGB is prosecuting the s11 line against PLAs that licensed 'online gaming' products and is procuring blocking capability; the Communications Minister is testing an Icasa network-level route; and the DA — a GNU partner — both sponsors the Remote Gambling Bill to legalise and regulate remote gambling and opposes the 20% tax. Provinces, which collect R6.45bn (~$391m) and rely on gambling for scarce own revenue, are the natural counterweight to both a national levy and advertising curbs. The courts are an active venue: the casino lobby won at the SCA, and the lottery licence award to Sizekhaya was set aside by the Pretoria High Court on 3 November 2026.

For an operator, the direction of travel is a tighter perimeter (sports and lawful contingencies only), a heavier fiscal load (from ~18–20% all-in to a plausible 30–40% of GGR from FY2027/28), narrower marketing (sponsorship and watershed limits), and — eventually — better-protected licensed demand if blocking and payment interdiction work. The asymmetry is timing: the tax and ad rules are 2027 events with high probability; blocking and online-casino legalisation are 2027–2028 events with lower probability. A market-entry case should therefore be built on sports-betting economics under the higher tax scenario, with the online-casino option valued at zero until a national remote licence exists.

highlights.text: Scale and momentum: Africa's largest regulated market at R84.46bn (~$5.12bn) GGR, with disclosed online betting GGR of R55.77bn (~$3.38bn) growing 25.4% and betting stakes of R1.40tn (~$84.9bn) up 24.5% — a legal, bankable online sports-betting pool larger than most European mid-tier markets.

Low headline fiscal load today: provincial bookmaker tax of ~6.5% of GGR (+1% levy) plus 15% VAT — an effective 6.6% provincial take in FY25/26 and roughly 18–20% all-in — with no player-winnings withholding, versus 20–40%+ in many benchmark jurisdictions.

Payments and distribution are ready-made: 91% of digital wagering is mobile, settlement runs on cards, instant EFT and retail vouchers with no telco revenue share, and 315 licensed bookmakers show the licence is obtainable — Western Cape and Mpumalanga process quickly at immaterial fees (R15,000/~$910 application, trade-press figure).

Provincial licensing arbitrage is real and legal: a licence from any province serves punters nationwide; Eastern Cape (+676%) and North West (+205%) betting GGR show new domiciles opening up, and effective betting tax ranges from 5.0% (NW) to 10.5% (KZN).

Enforcement is tilting toward the licensed channel: SCA/NRCS have levelled the product perimeter across licensed books, 27 illegal sites have been restricted, a national monitoring/blocking tender closed 4 Sep 2026, and FIC/SABRIC/SARB payment cooperation is being formalised — if delivered, licensed demand recaptures part of the estimated R50bn (~$3.0bn) offshore pool.

B2B demand from incumbents: casino groups are redeploying into digital (SunBet income +35.5% to R1.18bn/~$72m in H1-2026 vs market ~19%; Sun land-based share 49%), and a fragmented long tail of ~310 smaller bookmakers facing a possible tax doubling will need platform, trading and compliance outsourcing or exits.

Horse racing is an unexpected growth niche: bookmaker horse-racing GGR +36.9% to R4.81bn (~$292m), concentrated in the Western Cape, at a 9.2% effective tax — a differentiated vertical where the duopoly is less dominant.

lowlights.text: Tax cliff: Treasury's 20% national online GGR tax (additional to provincial tax and VAT) would lift the all-in burden from ~18–20% to ~38–40% of GGR, equivalent to >R10bn (~$606m) p.a.; final design in the Feb-2027 Budget. Even a diluted 10–15% version would compress bookmaker margins by 10–15pp on a ~4% hold product.

No online casino, and the workaround is gone: s11 prohibits interactive gambling, the SCA (21 Oct 2025) barred fixed-odds casino games for bookmakers, and NRCS stopped certifying Remote Gaming Servers. Gauteng betting GGR fell 19.2% and its RTP dropped from 88% to 61% — a preview for any province where 'online gaming' products are challenged. No remote-gambling legislation before 2027.

Entrenched duopoly: Betway and Hollywoodbets held >75% of online demand (Blask, Mar-2025), with Betway still gaining share; the top three brands take ~50% of 380m quarterly site visits; both leaders own football title sponsorships, the marketing channel most exposed to the coming advertising rules.

Illegal market the size of the legal one: industry estimates put ~62% of online activity offshore, >R50bn (~$3.0bn) GGR and ~16m users, with the NGB admitting it has no blocking architecture; a higher tax on the licensed channel widens the price gap with untaxed offshore sites.

Advertising and RG tightening with unclear scope: dtic's national advertising norms/regulations (promised before July 2026) are overdue, a ban-the-ads/sponsorships campaign is active, the National Self-Exclusion Register is still inoperative and the NGB is publicly flagging NSFAS and SASSA recipients — affordability-style controls could follow.

Regulatory fragmentation and governance: nine PLAs with divergent rules, an open NGB–PLA s11 dispute before the Policy Council, the NGB completing only 9 of 45 planned PLA compliance evaluations, Gauteng statistics provisional/unaudited, and online/retail splits for six provinces only — material data and legal-certainty gaps for underwriting.

Growth is decelerating: betting GGR growth has stepped down from +51.2% to +44.7% to +19.6%, Q3 FY25/26 was +13.8%, and hold is drifting lower (RTP 95.6%); entrants are arriving as the market matures and a Treasury-designed 'sin tax' is explicitly intended to reduce volumes.

forecast.intro: The primary release (NGB audited statistics, 3 Nov 2026) shows a regulated base still compounding at +13% while the rule-set is rewritten around it. The bridge from FY2025/26 to our FY2026/27 outlook is driven by one division — online sports betting in the Mpumalanga and Western Cape licence hubs — and by three regulatory moving parts: the Feb-2027 Budget decision on the 20% national online GGR tax (effective no earlier than FY2027/28 given money-bill procedure), the overdue dtic advertising norms and regulations, and the NGB's blocking-vendor appointment. Nothing in the pipeline legalises online casino before 2027, and the SCA/NRCS actions remove the grey-product tailwind that flattered FY24/25.

bridge.title: Online/retail betting FY26/27E (+15–19%; estimate)
bridge.change: Sports-led; no casino-style content; Q3 base effect

forecast.view: Our independent view: regulated GGR of **R93–96bn (~$5.6–5.8bn) in FY2026/27 (estimate)**, with betting above 76% of the total and disclosed online above 70%, then a step-down in FY2027/28 if the national tax is enacted at or near 20% (we would model licensed betting GGR growth falling to low single digits and 20–30% of the 315 bookmakers exiting or consolidating). On the tax itself, our base case is that **a national online levy is enacted but below the 20% headline or phased** — the money-bill route, DA opposition inside the GNU, provincial revenue dependence and Treasury's own Kenya caveat all argue for dilution; we put the probability of 20% as proposed, effective 1 April 2027, at roughly one in three [judgement]. All-in operator burden moves from ~18–20% of GGR to **30–40%** in the adverse case. Advertising: **norms and standards gazetted by H1-2027 with watershed, sponsorship-disclosure and bonus-advertising limits rather than a ban**. Online casino: **no lawful product before 2028**; the Remote Gambling Bill will not pass in 2027 and the NGB's s11 posture, now backed by the SCA, will be extended to lucky-numbers and virtual products in other provinces via the Policy Council. Enforcement: a blocking vendor appointed in 2027 with ISP-level blocking contested in court; payment interdiction via FIC/SABRIC is the more effective lever. Leverage direction for the market is **toward consolidation**: fee-light licensing keeps entry cheap, but a ~4% hold product facing a possible 20pp tax increase and tighter marketing favours scale players (Betway, Hollywoodbets, SunBet) and B2B suppliers over new B2C brands.
watch: Feb-2027 Budget: rate, base (online betting only vs all online incl. lucky numbers/virtuals), effective date, SARS administration and interaction with provincial taxes; then passage through the NA and NCOP finance committees as a money bill.

dtic national advertising norms & standards and gambling advertising regulations (promised before Jul-2026, still pending): watershed, sports-sponsorship, influencer and bonus-ad rules; any Icasa/ECA-based measures and legal challenges.
NGB monitoring/blocking vendor appointment following the EOI that closed 4 Sep 2026; MOUs with SABRIC/SARB; bank card-blocking of offshore gambling MCCs.

National Gambling Policy Council determination on the NGB–PLA s11 dispute and any follow-on litigation extending the SCA logic to lucky numbers, virtuals and 'betgames' outside Gauteng; NRCS treatment of existing RGS certifications on expiry.
Lottery: appeal or re-tender after the 3 Nov 2026 High Court ruling setting aside Sizekhaya's licence; interim operator arrangements and any read-across to NLC/dtic licensing credibility.

Quarterly NGB data: audited Gauteng restatement, extension of the online/retail split to Gauteng, KZN and Free State, and FY26/27 H1 betting growth versus the +23% comparatives (deceleration below +15% would confirm maturity).

Operator moves: Betway/Hollywoodbets share, SunBet and Tsogo digital growth, mid-tier M&A (Supabets, WSB, LottoStar, YesPlay), and any licence migration into Eastern Cape/North West; Remote Gambling Bill and National Gambling Amendment Bill scheduling; activation of the National Self-Exclusion Register.

report.confidenceNote: Core market figures are HIGH confidence: taken directly from the NGB's audited FY2025/26 National Gambling Statistics (3 Nov 2026) and NGB Annual Report 2025/26, cross-checked against the FY2024/25 NGB release and against Gaming Intelligence, The Citizen, News24/GroundUp and Daily Maverick (all report R84.46bn GGR, R62.16bn betting, R6.45bn tax, R1.76tn turnover). Caveats: the NGB flags Gauteng data as provisional/unaudited; the online/retail split is disclosed for six provinces only, so the 66% online share is a floor. FX: USD/ZAR 16.5 used throughout — this is an ESTIMATE, not a dated market rate: the research tool quota was exhausted before a rate for 3 Nov 2026 could be retrieved; it is implied from Gaming Intelligence's EUR conversion of the same release (R84.46bn = €4.43bn → EUR/ZAR ≈19.1 on ~23 Nov 2026) and an assumed EUR/USD ≈1.16. Treat all ~USD figures as indicative (±5%) and rescale as needed. Unverified/secondary: Western Cape licence-fee figures (trade press only); Blask demand-share and traffic-share estimates (not GGR shares); Yield Sec/CGCSA illegal-market estimates (industry-commissioned); the current parliamentary status of the Remote Gambling Bill (sources conflict on lapse/revival); the statutory 40-casino cap (from the Act, not re-read in this exercise). FY2026/27 figures in the forecast are our estimates.
